title: Ang 349–360: Nanak in Asa
hookLine: ask about the light, not the caste, on ang 349
tomorrow: what did Guru Nanak say to God when the soldiers came?

cards: Meeting someone new comes with a script: what's your name, where are you from, what do you do. In some families there's one more question, asked a little quieter, about what group they come from.
On ang 349, Guru Nanak gives a different first question. In paraphrase: recognize the light; don't ask about caste; ahead, there is no caste. Not where someone comes from.

teach.h: JOT IS LIGHT. JAAT IS CASTE.
teach.b: The word for light here is jot, the light of the One in every being. The word for caste is jaat, the group you're born into. Say them aloud: jot, jaat.

Guru Nanak sets them side by side and makes you choose which one your eyes go to first. Caste sorted people by birth: who ate with whom, who could come in where. This line doesn't argue with it for pages.

teach.h: THE SAME FLAME IN ANY LAMP.
teach.b: A flame doesn't change with the lamp it sits in. Clay, brass, a jar on a windowsill: the same light.
And ahead, the line says, after this life, there's no caste at all, so the ranking was never going to last. Sikhs carry this into the gurdwara.
In the langar everyone sits on the same floor and eats the same food, whoever they are.
And if a child asks at dinner why that matters, here's a sentence that fits: everyone has the same light inside, and that's the first thing to look for.

how: In the gurdwara's langar, everyone who comes sits together on the floor and is served the same meal, whatever their background; the Sikh Rehat Maryada rejects distinctions of caste among Sikhs.

o: Guru Nanak's page: seek the light, not caste
the page where Raag Asa begins with So Dar
the page of Ravidas's city without sorrow

games.q: the light, not caste — tap the pairs.
p: the light of the One in everyone
caste: the group you're born into
the same floor, the same food

s: Guru Nanak's line is only about the afterlife
it says recognize the light now, don't ask caste; and ahead, there's no caste either.
jot and jaat sound almost alike
light and caste, one breath apart; the line asks which one your eyes go to first.
langar seats people by family background
everyone sits on the same floor and eats the same food.

games.q: a new kid joins your team, and before anyone learns his name, someone asks what he is. what fits ang 349?
o: ask his name and what he loves; look for the light first.
find out his background first, so you know where he fits.
keep your distance until the team decides about him.
games.why: Guru Nanak: recognize the light, don't ask the caste. the first question is about the person, not the group.

practice: Light a candle or a small lamp if it's safe, or look at any light near you: a bulb, the window, a screen turned down low. Read ang 349 first if you can.
Then watch the light for the whole sit, and notice it shines the same whatever it's shining from.

wordCard.voice: Ang 349. The page of Guru Nanak's Asa hymn that says: recognize the light, don't ask the caste.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: jot, light; set beside jaat, caste, on ang 349.

carryVoice: Carry this: the light, not caste, the first thing to look for in anyone. Back tomorrow.
